questions.prompt: What problem do generics solve that `any` does not?

options.text: They preserve the relationship between types (e.g. input to output), keeping full type safety

questions.explanation: A type parameter captures the caller's type and reuses it, so information (like input relating to output) is preserved — unlike any, which discards it.

questions.prompt: Do you usually pass type arguments explicitly, like `identity<string>('hi')`?

options.text: No — TypeScript infers the type argument from the value; you specify it only when inference can't
Type arguments are never allowed explicitly

questions.explanation: Type arguments are usually inferred from the values you pass; you supply them explicitly only when inference cannot determine them.

questions.prompt: To limit a type parameter so you can use a property inside a generic, you add a constraint with the ______ keyword. (one word)
questions.explanation: A constraint like <T extends { length: number }> guarantees T has the needed members, so you can safely use them.

questions.prompt: How do you make `getProperty(obj, key)` reject keys that don't exist on obj?

options.text: Constrain the key: <T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]

questions.explanation: K extends keyof T limits key to real keys of T, and T[K] returns the exact value type — so invalid keys are compile errors.

questions.prompt: When is adding a type parameter NOT worth it?

options.text: When it connects an input to an output
When it appears only once and carries no relationship — a concrete type is clearer
Type parameters are always worth adding

questions.explanation: A type parameter earns its place by connecting positions (input to output, key to value). Used once with no relationship, it just adds noise.

questions.prompt: Which can be generic in TypeScript? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Functions, interfaces, and classes can all take type parameters. A boolean literal is a value/type, not something parameterized.
